## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 What is a Symbol?

A **symbol** is the most primitive, indivisible, atomic object from which strings are built. It cannot be broken down into smaller meaningful units within the context of formal language theory. Symbols are abstract entities — letters, digits, punctuation marks, or even graphical icons.

> [!NOTE]
> **Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus):**
> A *symbol* is any single, indivisible entity (character, letter, digit, or pictograph) used as a building block to form strings over an alphabet.

---

### 1.2 What is an Alphabet (Σ)?

An **alphabet** is a finite, non-empty set of symbols. It is the universe from which we draw characters to construct strings.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Why must Σ be non-empty?**
> If $\Sigma = \emptyset$, then the only string we can form is the empty string $\varepsilon$, which defeats the purpose of building a rich language. Hence, by KTU convention and standard formal language theory, an alphabet must contain **at least one** symbol.

**Standard Examples of Alphabets:**

| Notation | Alphabet | Common Usage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\{a, b\}$ | Binary-style toy alphabets |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\{0, 1\}$ | Digital / Boolean alphabets |
| $\Sigma_3$ | $\{a, b, \dots, z\}$ | Lowercase English letters |
| $\Sigma_4$ | ASCII | Computer character encoding |

---

### 1.3 What is a String (Word)?

A **string** (also called a **word** or **sentence** in some textbooks) is a finite sequence of symbols drawn from a given alphabet $\Sigma$. The order of symbols matters, and repetitions are allowed.

> [!NOTE]
> **Formal Definition:**
> A *string* over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is a finite ordered sequence $w = w_1 w_2 w_3 \dots w_n$ where each $w_i \in \Sigma$ and $n \geq 0$.

---

### 1.4 Conceptual Analogy — "Strings are Sentences in a Secret Language"

Imagine alphabets as the **scattered letters of a magnet set on your fridge**.

- Each individual letter tile = a **symbol**.
- The set of all tiles you own = the **alphabet** $\Sigma$.
- When you line up a few tiles in a row to spell "CAT" = a **string**.
- The set of all valid English words your kid can spell = a **language** $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$.

The key idea: **you cannot put a tile on the fridge that you don't own**, and you must use tiles in a specific order to convey meaning — exactly how strings are formed over alphabets in Theory of Computation.

> [!TIP]
> **KTU Quick Intuition:** A symbol is a *raw material*, an alphabet is a *toolbox*, and a string is a *product* assembled using the tools in a specific order.

---

### 1.5 The Empty String ($\varepsilon$ or $\lambda$)

The **empty string** is a string with **zero** symbols. It is denoted $\varepsilon$ (epsilon) or $\lambda$ (lambda). Although it contains nothing, it is still a perfectly valid string over *any* alphabet.

$$w = \varepsilon \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{length} \mid w \mid = 0$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Common KTU Mistake:** The empty string $\varepsilon$ is **NOT** the empty set $\emptyset$. The empty set has no elements, whereas the empty set of symbols *is* a valid string with length zero. They are fundamentally different objects.

---

### 1.6 Quick Hierarchy of Formal Language Objects

$$\text{Symbols} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Alphabet } (\Sigma) \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Strings } (\Sigma^*) \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Languages } (L \subseteq \Sigma^*)$$

This pipeline is foundational: every concept in TOC — finite automata, regular expressions, grammars, Turing machines — is ultimately built atop this hierarchy.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Length of a String

The **length** of a string $w$, denoted $\vert w \vert$, is the number of symbols it contains. For the empty string, the length is **0**.

$$\vert w \vert = n \quad \text{where} \quad w = w_1 w_2 \dots w_n$$

**Example:**
If $w = \texttt{10110}$, then $\vert w \vert = 5$.

---

### 2.2 Concatenation of Strings

Concatenation is the operation of **gluing** two strings end-to-end. It is denoted by simple juxtaposition (no symbol) or sometimes by a dot $\cdot$.

$$x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m, \quad y = y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$$

$$xy = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$$

**Key Property (Length of Concatenation):**
$$\vert xy \vert = \vert x \vert + \vert y \vert$$

**Identity Element:** The empty string $\varepsilon$ is the identity for concatenation:
$$w \varepsilon = \varepsilon w = w$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU High-Yield Property:** Concatenation is **associative** but **NOT commutative** in general. That is, $(xy)z = x(yz)$, but $xy \neq yx$ unless $x = y$ or one of them is $\varepsilon$.

---

### 2.3 Power of a String (Repetition)

For any string $w$ and non-negative integer $n \geq 0$, the $n$-th power of $w$ is $w$ concatenated with itself $n$ times.

$$w^n = \underbrace{w \cdot w \cdot w \cdots w}_{n \text{ times}}$$

**Recursive Definition:**
$$w^0 = \varepsilon, \quad w^{n+1} = w^n \cdot w$$

**Example:** If $w = \texttt{ab}$, then:
- $w^0 = \varepsilon$
- $w^1 = \texttt{ab}$
- $w^2 = \texttt{abab}$
- $w^3 = \texttt{ababab}$

**Length Property:**
$$\vert w^n \vert = n \cdot \vert w \vert$$

---

### 2.4 Reverse of a String

The **reverse** of a string $w$, denoted $w^R$, is $w$ written backwards. Symbol at position $i$ moves to position $n - i + 1$.

$$w = w_1 w_2 \dots w_n \quad \Longrightarrow \quad w^R = w_n w_{n-1} \dots w_1$$

**Examples:**
- $w = \texttt{101}$, $w^R = \texttt{101}$ (palindrome)
- $w = \texttt{hello}$, $w^R = \texttt{olleh}$

**Properties:**
- $\varepsilon^R = \varepsilon$
- $(xy)^R = y^R x^R$ (anti-homomorphism — order reverses!)
- $(w^R)^R = w$
- $\vert w^R \vert = \vert w \vert$

---

### 2.5 Kleene Closure ($\Sigma^*$) and Positive Closure ($\Sigma^+$)

These are the two most important set-of-strings operators in TOC.

**Kleene Star $\Sigma^*$:** Set of **all** strings (including $\varepsilon$) over $\Sigma$ of any finite length.

$$\Sigma^* = \Sigma^0 \cup \Sigma^1 \cup \Sigma^2 \cup \dots = \bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty} \Sigma^i$$

**Positive Closure $\Sigma^+$:**
$$\Sigma^+ = \Sigma^1 \cup \Sigma^2 \cup \dots = \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} \Sigma^i$$

**Fundamental Relation:**
$$\Sigma^+ = \Sigma^* - \{\varepsilon\}$$

> [!CAUTION]
> **KTU Pitfall:** $\Sigma^*$ is **infinite** even if $\Sigma$ is finite, because there is no upper bound on string length. For $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, $\Sigma^*$ contains $\varepsilon, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, aaa, \dots$ — countably infinite.

---

### 2.6 Substrings, Prefixes, and Suffixes

For a string $w = x y z$ (where $x, y, z$ are substrings):

- **Prefix:** $x$ (any leading segment) or $\varepsilon$.
- **Suffix:** $z$ (any trailing segment) or $\varepsilon$.
- **Substring:** $y$ (any contiguous block) or $\varepsilon$.
- **Proper prefix/suffix/substring:** A non-trivial one ($\neq w$).

> [!TIP]
> Every string is both a prefix and a suffix of **itself**, and $\varepsilon$ is a prefix/suffix/substring of **every** string.

---

### 2.7 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Concept | Notation | Formula / Rule | Key Property |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Length of string | $\vert w \vert$ | Number of symbols in $w$ | $\vert \varepsilon \vert = 0$ |
| 2 | Concatenation | $xy$ | Glue $x$ and $y$ end-to-end | $\vert xy \vert = \vert x \vert + \vert y \vert$ |
| 3 | Identity element | $\varepsilon$ | $w \varepsilon = \varepsilon w = w$ | Length $= 0$ |
| 4 | String power | $w^n$ | $w$ repeated $n$ times | $\vert w^n \vert = n \cdot \vert w \vert$ |
| 5 | Reverse | $w^R$ | Reverse symbol order | $(xy)^R = y^R x^R$ |
| 6 | Kleene star | $\Sigma^*$ | All strings of length $\geq 0$ | $\varepsilon \in \Sigma^*$ always |
| 7 | Positive closure | $\Sigma^+$ | All strings of length $\geq 1$ | $\Sigma^+ = \Sigma^* \setminus \{\varepsilon\}$ |
| 8 | Concatenation associativity | $(xy)z$ | $= x(yz)$ | Always holds |
| 9 | Distributive over union | $x(L \cup M)$ | $= xL \cup xM$ | Important for languages |
| 10 | Palindrome condition | $w$ | $w = w^R$ | Reads same forwards/backwards |

---

### 2.8 Real-World Utility in Engineering

- **Compilers & Lexical Analyzers:** Tokenizing source code into strings of symbols, then matching patterns via regex (which is built on $\Sigma^*$, $\Sigma^+$).
- **Network Protocols:** Every transmitted packet is essentially a string over an alphabet of bytes $\{0, 1, \dots, 255\}^{256}$.
- **Bioinformatics:** DNA sequences are strings over $\Sigma = \{A, C, G, T\}$; pattern matching algorithms work directly on these strings.
- **Database Systems:** String operations form the basis of text-search engines (LIKE queries, full-text indexing).
- **Cryptography:** Plaintexts and ciphertexts are modeled as strings; security proofs (IND-CPA) are framed over $\Sigma^*$.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Length of a Concatenated String

**Statement:** For any two strings $x, y$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, $\vert xy \vert = \vert x \vert + \vert y \vert$.

**Proof (by direct construction):**

Let $x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m$ and $y = y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$ where $m = \vert x \vert$ and $n = \vert y \vert$.

By definition of concatenation:
$$xy = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m \, y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$$

Counting symbols: there are $m$ symbols from $x$ followed by $n$ symbols from $y$, in total:

$$\begin{aligned}
\vert xy \vert &= m + n \\
&= \vert x \vert + \vert y \vert
\end{aligned}$$

Hence proved. $\blacksquare$

---

### 3.2 Derivation: Length of String Power

**Statement:** For any string $w$ and integer $n \geq 0$, $\vert w^n \vert = n \cdot \vert w \vert$.

**Proof (by mathematical induction on $n$):**

**Base Case ($n = 0$):**
$$\vert w^0 \vert = \vert \varepsilon \vert = 0 = 0 \cdot \vert w \vert \quad \checkmark$$

**Inductive Step:** Assume true for $n = k$, i.e., $\vert w^k \vert = k \cdot \vert w \vert$.

For $n = k + 1$:
$$\begin{aligned}
\vert w^{k+1} \vert &= \vert w^k \cdot w \vert \\
&= \vert w^k \vert + \vert w \vert \quad \text{(by length-of-concatenation property)} \\
&= k \cdot \vert w \vert + \vert w \vert \quad \text{(by inductive hypothesis)} \\
&= (k + 1) \cdot \vert w \vert
\end{aligned}$$

Hence proved by induction. $\blacksquare$

---

### 3.3 Derivation: Reverse of a Concatenation

**Statement:** $(xy)^R = y^R x^R$

**Proof:**

Let $x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m$ and $y = y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$.

Then:
$$xy = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m \, y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$$

Now reverse:
$$(xy)^R = y_n y_{n-1} \dots y_1 \, x_m x_{m-1} \dots x_1$$

Group the $y$'s and $x$'s:
$$(xy)^R = (y_n y_{n-1} \dots y_1)(x_m x_{m-1} \dots x_1) = y^R \cdot x^R$$

Hence proved. $\blacksquare$

---

### 3.4 Worked Example 1: Operation Cascade

**Problem:** Let $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$, $w = \texttt{01}$, $x = \texttt{110}$. Compute $w^2 x^R$.

**Step 1:** Compute $w^2$
$$w^2 = w \cdot w = \texttt{01} \cdot \texttt{01} = \texttt{0101}$$

**Step 2:** Compute $x^R$
$$x = \texttt{110} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x^R = \texttt{011}$$

**Step 3:** Concatenate
$$w^2 x^R = \texttt{0101} \cdot \texttt{011} = \texttt{0101011}$$

**Verification (length check):**
$$\begin{aligned}
\vert w^2 x^R \vert &= \vert w^2 \vert + \vert x^R \vert \\
&= 2 \cdot \vert w \vert + \vert x \vert \\
&= 2(2) + 3 \\
&= 7
\end{aligned}$$

Counting: $\texttt{0101011}$ has 7 symbols. ✓

---

### 3.5 Worked Example 2: Identifying Prefixes, Suffixes, Substrings

**Problem:** For $w = \texttt{banana}$, list all proper prefixes, proper suffixes, and a few substrings.

**Proper Prefixes** (excluding $w$ itself and $\varepsilon$):
$$\{\texttt{b}, \texttt{ba}, \texttt{ban}, \texttt{bana}, \texttt{banan}\}$$

**Proper Suffixes** (excluding $w$ itself and $\varepsilon$):
$$\{\texttt{a}, \texttt{na}, \texttt{ana}, \texttt{nana}, \texttt{anana}\}$$

**Substrings** (contiguous, including non-trivial ones):
$$\{\texttt{b}, \texttt{a}, \texttt{n}, \texttt{ba}, \texttt{an}, \texttt{na}, \texttt{ban}, \texttt{ana}, \texttt{nan}, \texttt{bana}, \texttt{anan}, \texttt{nana}, \dots\}$$

> [!NOTE]
> Every prefix and suffix is also a substring, but not every substring is a prefix or suffix. Substrings are the most general category.

---

### 3.6 Worked Example 3: Kleene Closure Enumeration

**Problem:** Enumerate the first 8 elements of $\Sigma^*$ for $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, grouped by length.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Length 0:} \quad & \varepsilon \\
\text{Length 1:} \quad & a, \; b \\
\text{Length 2:} \quad & aa, \; ab, \; ba, \; bb \\
\text{Length 3:} \quad & aaa, \; aab, \; aba, \; abb, \; baa, \; bab, \; bba, \; bbb
\end{aligned}$$

Total count up to length 3:
$$1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 \text{ strings}$$

**General Formula:** The number of distinct strings in $\Sigma^*$ with length exactly $n$ is $\vert \Sigma \vert^n$. Hence, the number of strings with length $\leq n$ is the geometric sum:
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \vert \Sigma \vert^i = \frac{\vert \Sigma \vert^{n+1} - 1}{\vert \Sigma \vert - 1} \quad (\text{for } \vert \Sigma \vert > 1)$$

For $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, $\vert \Sigma \vert = 2$, and strings of length $\leq 3$:
$$\frac{2^4 - 1}{2 - 1} = \frac{15}{1} = 15 \checkmark$$

---

### 3.7 Worked Example 4: Palindrome Test Using Reverse

**Problem:** Determine whether $w = \texttt{racecar}$ is a palindrome.

**Method:** Compute $w^R$ and compare to $w$.

$$w^R = \texttt{racecar}^R = \texttt{racecar}$$

Since $w^R = w$, the string $w$ is a palindrome. ✓

**Counter-example:** $w = \texttt{computer}$

$$w^R = \texttt{retupmoc} \neq \texttt{computer}$$

Hence $\texttt{computer}$ is **not** a palindrome.

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

#### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
**Define the following with one example each:**
**(i)** Alphabet
**(ii)** String
**(iii)** Kleene Closure

**Model Answer:**

**(i) Alphabet:** A finite, non-empty set of symbols, denoted $\Sigma$. It is the universe of allowed characters for constructing strings.
*Example:* $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$

**(ii) String:** A finite ordered sequence of symbols drawn from an alphabet $\Sigma$.
*Example:* $w = \texttt{0101}$ over $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$

**(iii) Kleene Closure ($\Sigma^*$):** The set of all strings (of any finite length, including the empty string) that can be formed over $\Sigma$.
*Example:* For $\Sigma = \{a\}$, $\Sigma^* = \{\varepsilon, a, aa, aaa, \dots\}$

> [!NOTE]
> **Valuation Tip:** Always give the **symbolic notation** *and* a concrete **example** in the same line — examiners reward the pairing (1 mark each: definition + example).

---

#### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – June 2024]**
**State and explain any three properties of string concatenation.**

**Model Answer:**

**Property 1 — Closure:** Concatenation of two strings over $\Sigma$ yields a string over $\Sigma$.
If $x, y \in \Sigma^*$, then $xy \in \Sigma^*$.

**Property 2 — Associativity:** For any three strings $x, y, z \in \Sigma^*$,
$$(xy)z = x(yz)$$
*Example:* $x = \texttt{a}, \; y = \texttt{b}, \; z = \texttt{c}$ → $(\texttt{ab})\texttt{c} = \texttt{abc} = \texttt{a}(\texttt{bc})$ ✓

**Property 3 — Identity Element:** The empty string $\varepsilon$ is the identity element.
$$w \varepsilon = \varepsilon w = w \quad \text{for all } w \in \Sigma^*$$

**Property 4 (bonus):** Non-commutativity in general.
$$xy \neq yx \quad \text{unless } x = y \text{ or one is } \varepsilon$$
*Example:* $\texttt{ab} \neq \texttt{ba}$

> [!TIP]
> For full 3 marks, present at least **three** properties with their *symbolic statement* and *one example each*.

### **Question A (14 Marks)**

#### **Q.A. (a) [7 Marks]**
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2022 / June 2023 pattern]**
Let $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$. For each of the following strings, compute $\vert w \vert$, $w^R$, and $w^2$:
**(i)** $w_1 = \texttt{abba}$
**(ii)** $w_2 = \texttt{bab}$
**(iii)** $w_3 = \varepsilon$

**Model Solution:**

**(i) $w_1 = \texttt{abba}$**

Length:
$$\vert w_1 \vert = 4$$

Reverse (write backwards):
$$w_1^R = \texttt{abba}$$

(Notice: $w_1^R = w_1$ — this is a **palindrome**.)

Power:
$$w_1^2 = w_1 \cdot w_1 = \texttt{abba} \cdot \texttt{abba} = \texttt{abbaabba}$$

Verification of length: $\vert w_1^2 \vert = 2 \cdot 4 = 8$ ✓

---

**(ii) $w_2 = \texttt{bab}$**

Length:
$$\vert w_2 \vert = 3$$

Reverse:
$$w_2^R = \texttt{bab}$$

(Palindrome again — symmetric around the central $\texttt{a}$.)

Power:
$$w_2^2 = \texttt{bab} \cdot \texttt{bab} = \texttt{babbab}$$

Verification: $\vert w_2^2 \vert = 2 \cdot 3 = 6$ ✓

---

**(iii) $w_3 = \varepsilon$**

Length:
$$\vert \varepsilon \vert = 0$$

Reverse:
$$\varepsilon^R = \varepsilon$$

Power:
$$\varepsilon^2 = \varepsilon \cdot \varepsilon = \varepsilon$$

Verification: $\vert \varepsilon^2 \vert = 2 \cdot 0 = 0$ ✓

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout:** Students often write $w^2 = 2w$ or use arithmetic multiplication. **Concatenation is NOT arithmetic multiplication.** $w^2$ means $w$ written twice side-by-side, not $2$ times the numerical value. Loss of **2 marks** is common here.

---

#### **Q.A. (b) [7 Marks]**
**[KTU University Exam – May 2024 pattern]**
Define the **Kleene Closure** $\Sigma^*$ and **Positive Closure** $\Sigma^+$ of an alphabet. With $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$, enumerate the first 10 elements of $\Sigma^*$ in increasing order of length, and state the relationship between $\Sigma^*$ and $\Sigma^+$.

**Model Solution:**

**Definitions:**

- **Kleene Closure $\Sigma^*$:** The set of all strings of any finite length (including the empty string) over $\Sigma$.
$$\Sigma^* = \bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty} \Sigma^i \quad \text{where } \Sigma^i = \{w : \vert w \vert = i\}$$

- **Positive Closure $\Sigma^+$:**
$$\Sigma^+ = \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} \Sigma^i = \Sigma^* \setminus \{\varepsilon\}$$

**Enumeration of $\Sigma^*$ for $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$** (in order of increasing length):

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Length 0:} \quad & \varepsilon \\
\text{Length 1:} \quad & 0, \; 1 \\
\text{Length 2:} \quad & 00, \; 01, \; 10, \; 11 \\
\text{Length 3:} \quad & 000, \; 001, \; 010, \; 011 \\
\text{(partial Length 4):} \quad & 1000, \; 1001
\end{aligned}$$

This is the first 10 elements:
$$\{\varepsilon, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, 001, 010\}$$

**Relationship between $\Sigma^*$ and $\Sigma^+$:**
$$\Sigma^+ = \Sigma^* - \{\varepsilon\}$$

That is, $\Sigma^+$ is $\Sigma^*$ with the empty string removed. Equivalently:
$$\Sigma^* = \Sigma^+ \cup \{\varepsilon\}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Valuation Tip (3 marks reserved for the relationship):** Explicitly state the formula $\Sigma^+ = \Sigma^* \setminus \{\varepsilon\}$ and demonstrate with a small example that $\varepsilon \in \Sigma^*$ but $\varepsilon \notin \Sigma^+$.

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

#### **Q.B. (a) [7 Marks]**
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 pattern]**
For the string $w = \texttt{computation}$:
**(i)** Find $\vert w \vert$.
**(ii)** List all proper prefixes of length $\geq 3$.
**(iii)** List all proper suffixes of length $\geq 3$.
**(iv)** Is $w$ a palindrome? Justify.

**Model Solution:**

**(i) Length of $w$:**
$$w = \texttt{c, o, m, p, u, t, a, t, i, o, n}$$
Counting: $\vert w \vert = 11$

---

**(ii) Proper prefixes of length $\geq 3$:**

A **proper prefix** is a prefix strictly shorter than $w$. List prefixes by chopping characters from the right:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Length 3:} \quad & \texttt{com} \\
\text{Length 4:} \quad & \texttt{comp} \\
\text{Length 5:} \quad & \texttt{compu} \\
\text{Length 6:} \quad & \texttt{comput} \\
\text{Length 7:} \quad & \texttt{computa} \\
\text{Length 8:} \quad & \texttt{computat} \\
\text{Length 9:} \quad & \texttt{computati} \\
\text{Length 10:} \quad & \texttt{computatio}
\end{aligned}$$

---

**(iii) Proper suffixes of length $\geq 3$:**

A **proper suffix** is a suffix strictly shorter than $w$. Chop characters from the left:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Length 3:} \quad & \texttt{ion} \\
\text{Length 4:} \quad & \texttt{tion} \\
\text{Length 5:} \quad & \texttt{ation} \\
\text{Length 6:} \quad & \texttt{tation} \\
\text{Length 7:} \quad & \texttt{utation} \\
\text{Length 8:} \quad & \texttt{putation} \\
\text{Length 9:} \quad & \texttt{mputation} \\
\text{Length 10:} \quad & \texttt{omputation}
\end{aligned}$$

---

**(iv) Palindrome test:**

Compute $w^R$:
$$w^R = \texttt{noitaretsu pmoc} \quad \text{Wait — recompute character by character.}$$

$$w = \texttt{c o m p u t a t i o n}$$

Reversed:
$$w^R = \texttt{n o i t a t u p m o c}$$

That is:
$$w^R = \texttt{noitatupmoc}$$

Since $w = \texttt{computation} \neq \texttt{noitatupmoc} = w^R$, the string is **not a palindrome**.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistake:** Do not confuse "palindrome" with the related but different concept of *reverse property*. A palindrome satisfies $w = w^R$, period. Also be careful: a string with **one symbol repeated** (e.g., $\texttt{aaa}$) is trivially a palindrome.

---

#### **Q.B. (b) [7 Marks]**
**[KTU University Exam – June 2022 / Model Paper pattern]**
State and prove the following:
**(i)** $\vert w^n \vert = n \cdot \vert w \vert$ for all $n \geq 0$.
**(ii)** $(xy)^R = y^R x^R$ for all strings $x, y$.

**Model Solution:**

**(i) Proof that $\vert w^n \vert = n \cdot \vert w \vert$**

**Proof by Induction on $n$:**

**Base Case ($n = 0$):**
$$\begin{aligned}
w^0 &= \varepsilon \quad \text{(by definition of string power)} \\
\therefore \vert w^0 \vert &= \vert \varepsilon \vert = 0 = 0 \cdot \vert w \vert
\end{aligned}$$
Base case holds. ✓

**Inductive Hypothesis:** Assume true for $n = k$:
$$\vert w^k \vert = k \cdot \vert w \vert$$

**Inductive Step ($n = k+1$):**
$$\begin{aligned}
\vert w^{k+1} \vert &= \vert w^k \cdot w \vert \\
&= \vert w^k \vert + \vert w \vert \quad \text{(length-of-concatenation property)} \\
&= k \cdot \vert w \vert + \vert w \vert \quad \text{(by inductive hypothesis)} \\
&= (k+1) \cdot \vert w \vert
\end{aligned}$$

Hence, by the principle of mathematical induction, the formula holds for all $n \geq 0$. $\blacksquare$

---

**(ii) Proof that $(xy)^R = y^R x^R$**

**Direct Proof:**

Let $x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m$ and $y = y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$.

By definition of concatenation:
$$xy = x_1 x_2 \dots x_m \, y_1 y_2 \dots y_n$$

By definition of reverse (reversing the entire sequence):
$$(xy)^R = y_n y_{n-1} \dots y_1 \, x_m x_{m-1} \dots x_1$$

Now observe the two halves:

- The first half $y_n y_{n-1} \dots y_1$ is precisely $y^R$ (reversal of $y$).
- The second half $x_m x_{m-1} \dots x_1$ is precisely $x^R$ (reversal of $x$).

Therefore:
$$(xy)^R = y^R \cdot x^R$$

Hence proved. $\blacksquare$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Examiner's Note (KTU Valuation Style):** Full 7 marks require **(1)** clear statement of the base case, **(2)** explicit inductive hypothesis, **(3)** correct algebraic manipulation in the inductive step, and **(4)** the concluding invocation of PMI. Skipping any of these costs 1–2 marks.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Where Students Lose Marks on "Strings"**
> 1. **Confusing $\varepsilon$ with $\emptyset$** — costs 1 mark almost every time it appears.
> 2. **Writing $w^2$ as $2w$** — this is a classic KTU board-exam blunder; $w^2$ is concatenation, not arithmetic.
> 3. **Forgetting that $\Sigma^*$ includes $\varepsilon$** — leads to wrong set-cardinality answers in counting questions.
> 4. **Treating concatenation as commutative** — it is **not**; $\texttt{ab} \neq \texttt{ba}$.
> 5. **Skipping the empty-string base case in induction** — examiners deduct **1 mark** specifically for missing the $n = 0$ step.
> 6. **Misnaming $w^R$ as $w^{-1}$** — there is **no** string-inverse operation; reverse is denoted $w^R$ only.

---

### 📌 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **Symbol:** Smallest atomic entity — a single character from an alphabet.
- **Alphabet $\Sigma$:** A *finite, non-empty* set of symbols. It is the allowed "vocabulary."
- **String $w$:** A *finite* ordered sequence of symbols from $\Sigma$. Order matters; repetitions allowed.
- **Empty string $\varepsilon$:** A valid string of length **0**. **It is not the empty set $\emptyset$.**
- **Length $\vert w \vert$:** Number of symbols in $w$. For the empty string, length is 0.
- **Concatenation $xy$:** End-to-end gluing. Associative, **not commutative**. Identity is $\varepsilon$.
- **Length property of concatenation:** $\vert xy \vert = \vert x \vert + \vert y \vert$.
- **Power $w^n$:** $w$ concatenated with itself $n$ times; $w^0 = \varepsilon$. Length: $\vert w^n \vert = n \cdot \vert w \vert$.
- **Reverse $w^R$:** $w$ written backwards. Anti-homomorphism: $(xy)^R = y^R x^R$. Involution: $(w^R)^R = w$.
- **Palindrome:** A string satisfying $w = w^R$ (e.g., $\texttt{aba}$, $\texttt{racecar}$, $\varepsilon$, any single symbol).
- **Kleene closure $\Sigma^*$:** Set of *all* finite strings over $\Sigma$, **including $\varepsilon$**.
- **Positive closure $\Sigma^+$:** Set of all finite strings of length $\geq 1$. **Excludes $\varepsilon$.**
- **Key relationship:** $\Sigma^+ = \Sigma^* \setminus \{\varepsilon\}$ and $\Sigma^* = \Sigma^+ \cup \{\varepsilon\}$.
- **Prefix / Suffix / Substring:** Prefix = leading segment; Suffix = trailing segment; Substring = any contiguous block. The empty string $\varepsilon$ qualifies as all three for any $w$.
- **Counting strings:** Number of distinct strings of length $n$ over $\Sigma$ is $\vert \Sigma \vert^n$.
- **Always remember:** $\Sigma^*$ is **infinite** even when $\Sigma$ is finite, because string length has no upper bound.

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PEAIT419 - INTRODUCTION TO THEORY OF COMPUTATION > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** NFA with Epsilon Transitions ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Definition of ε-NFA An **ε-NFA (Nondeterministic Finite Automaton with Epsilon Transitions)** is formally defined as a 5-tuple: $$E = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$$ where each component carries an extended meaning compared to a standard NFA: - **$Q$** — A finite, non-empty set of **states**. - **$\Sigma$** — A finite, non-empty set of **input symbols** (the alphabet). The symbol $\varepsilon$ (epsilon) is **NOT** part of $\Sigma$. - **$\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \rightarrow 2^Q$** — The **transition function**, which is defined for every state on every input symbol *and* on the empty string $\varepsilon$. The output is a set of states (a subset of $Q$). - **$q_0 \in Q$** — The designated **start state**. - **$F \subseteq Q$** — The set of **final (accepting) states**. > [!IMPORTANT] > The key distinguishing feature of an ε-NFA is the inclusion of $\varepsilon$ in the domain of the transition function $\delta$. A standard NFA only transitions on actual input symbols from $\Sigma$; an ε-NFA can change state **without consuming any input symbol**. ### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy > [!NOTE] > **Intuition: The "Free Teleport" Elevator** > > Imagine a building with rooms representing states, and doors between rooms representing transitions on input symbols. A normal NFA is like walking through doors — every step forward **must** consume one letter from a written note (the input string). > > An ε-NFA adds **magical teleporters** (the $\varepsilon$-transitions) between certain rooms. You may, at any time and without reading any symbol, instantly use a teleporter to jump to another room. The string is accepted if you can walk through the doors (reading the input) and use the teleporters (for free) such that you end up in an accepting room exactly when the last letter is read. ### 1.3 Epsilon Closure — The Heart of ε-NFA Since an automaton may take any number of free $\varepsilon$-jumps before or after reading a symbol, we must track the set of states reachable "for free" from a given state. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Definition — $\varepsilon$-closure of a state $q$:** > > The $\varepsilon$-closure of $q$, denoted **ECLOSE($q$)**, is the set of all states reachable from $q$ using **zero or more** $\varepsilon$-transitions. By convention, $q$ is always in its own $\varepsilon$-closure (zero $\varepsilon$-transitions = stay where you are). Formally, ECLOSE($q$) is the smallest set $S \subseteq Q$ satisfying both: - $q \in S$, **and** - For every $p \in S$, we have $\delta(p, \varepsilon) \subseteq S$. **Extension to a set of states:** For $P \subseteq Q$, $$\text{ECLOSE}(P) = \bigcup_{q \in P} \text{ECLOSE}(q)$$ **Worked Mini-Example:** Suppose $\delta(p, \varepsilon) = \{r\}$ and $\delta(r, \varepsilon) = \{s\}$, and no further $\varepsilon$-transitions exist. Then $\text{ECLOSE}(p) = \{p, r, s\}$. ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Operational Semantics — How an ε-NFA Processes a String When a string $w = w_1 w_2 \dots w_n$ is fed to an ε-NFA, the machine operates as follows: 1. **Initialisation:** The set of "current possible states" begins as $\text{ECLOSE}(\{q_0\})$ — we may freely teleport from the start state before reading anything. 2. **Read a symbol $w_i$:** From every state $p$ in the current set, we transition on $w_i$ to $\delta(p, w_i)$. The union of all such destinations, taken together, is then closed under $\varepsilon$ (since free teleports may occur after each symbol). 3. **Termination:** After reading the last symbol, the string is **accepted** if the resulting set of current states contains at least one final state from $F$. ### 2.2 The Extended Transition Function $\hat{\delta}$ To capture this precisely, define the **extended transition function** $\hat{\delta} : Q \times \Sigma^* \rightarrow 2^Q$ recursively: **Base case** (empty string): $$\hat{\delta}(q, \varepsilon) = \text{ECLOSE}(q)$$ **Inductive case** ($w = xa$, where $x \in \Sigma^*$, $a \in \Sigma$): $$\hat{\delta}(q, wa) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \,\in\, \hat{\delta}(q, w)} \delta(p, a)\right)$$ > [!NOTE] > **Intuition for $\hat{\delta}$:** It says — "To find all states reachable from $q$ on string $w$, first find all states reachable on the prefix, then take one step on the next symbol from each of those states, and finally close everything under free $\varepsilon$-jumps." The **language accepted** by an ε-NFA $E$ is: $$L(E) = \{\, w \in \Sigma^* \mid \hat{\delta}(q_0, w) \cap F \neq \varnothing \,\}$$ ### 2.3 KTU Formula / Cheat Sheet | Concept | Mathematical Expression | Notes | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | ε-NFA tuple | $(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ | $\delta$ defined on $Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\})$ | | ε-closure (state) | $\text{ECLOSE}(q) = \text{smallest set } S \text{ with } q \in S \text{ and } \delta(p, \varepsilon) \subseteq S \ \forall p \in S$ | Always includes $q$ itself | | ε-closure (set) | $\text{ECLOSE}(P) = \bigcup_{q \in P} \text{ECLOSE}(q)$ | Distributive over union | | Extended $\delta$ (base) | $\hat{\delta}(q, \varepsilon) = \text{ECLOSE}(q)$ | Empty string jumps freely | | Extended $\delta$ (step) | $\hat{\delta}(q, wa) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \hat{\delta}(q,w)} \delta(p, a)\right)$ | One symbol + free jumps | | Acceptance | $L(E) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* \mid \hat{\delta}(q_0, w) \cap F \neq \varnothing \}$ | Any final state reached | | Equivalence | Every ε-NFA $\equiv$ some NFA (no $\varepsilon$) | Constructive conversion exists | > [!IMPORTANT] > **Why ε-NFA matters in engineering:** ε-NFAs arise naturally when constructing automata from regular expressions via Thompson's construction — the standard pipeline used in lexical analysers (lex/flex), pattern matchers (`grep`), and the regex engines of every major programming language. The free $\varepsilon$-jumps elegantly encode the structural concatenation, union, and Kleene-star operations. ### 2.4 Properties and Theorems - **Closure under union, concatenation, Kleene-star:** If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are accepted by ε-NFAs $E_1$ and $E_2$, then $L_1 \cup L_2$, $L_1 L_2$, and $L_1^*$ are also accepted by some ε-NFA. - **Equivalence with NFA:** For every ε-NFA $E$, there exists a standard NFA $N$ (with no $\varepsilon$-transitions) such that $L(E) = L(N)$. The construction is algorithmic and is the cornerstone of the conversion covered in Section 3. - **Closure under reversal, intersection, complement:** Inherited from NFA/DFA theory. ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 The ε-Elimination Algorithm (ε-NFA → NFA) Given an ε-NFA $E = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$, we construct an equivalent NFA $N = (Q, \Sigma, \delta', q_0, F')$ as follows: **Step 1 — Compute ε-closure of every state.** For each $q \in Q$, compute $\text{ECLOSE}(q)$ by repeatedly adding states reachable via $\varepsilon$-transitions until no new state is added. **Step 2 — Define the new transition function $\delta'$.** For each $q \in Q$ and each $a \in \Sigma$: $$\delta'(q, a) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \,\in\, \text{ECLOSE}(q)} \delta(p, a)\right)$$ In words: "From $q$, first take all free $\varepsilon$-jumps to reach a set of states; from each of those, read the symbol $a$; then take free $\varepsilon$-jumps again." **Step 3 — Determine new final states.** $$F' = \{\, q \in Q \mid \text{ECLOSE}(q) \cap F \neq \varnothing \,\}$$ A state $q$ becomes final in the new NFA if any state reachable from $q$ via free $\varepsilon$-jumps was final in the original ε-NFA. ### 3.2 Exhaustive Worked Example **Problem.** Convert the following ε-NFA, which accepts the language $L = 0^* 1^*$ (any number of $0$s followed by any number of $1$s, including the empty string), into an equivalent NFA without $\varepsilon$-transitions. **Given components:** $$Q = \{q_0, q_1\}, \quad \Sigma = \{0, 1\}, \quad q_0 = \text{start}, \quad F = \{q_0, q_1\}$$ Transition function $\delta$: $$\delta(q_0, 0) = \{q_0\}, \quad \delta(q_0, 1) = \varnothing$$ $$\delta(q_1, 0) = \varnothing, \quad \delta(q_1, 1) = \{q_1\}$$ $$\delta(q_0, \varepsilon) = \{q_1\}, \quad \delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \varnothing$$ **Step 1 — Compute ε-closure of each state.** - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0)$: Start with $\{q_0\}$. From $q_0$, $\delta(q_0, \varepsilon) = \{q_1\}$, so add $q_1$. From $q_1$, $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \varnothing$, stop. Thus: $$\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) = \{q_0, q_1\}$$ - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_1)$: Start with $\{q_1\}$. From $q_1$, $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \varnothing$, stop. Thus: $$\text{ECLOSE}(q_1) = \{q_1\}$$ **Step 2 — Compute $\delta'$ for every state-symbol pair.** **For state $q_0$, symbol $0$:** $$\delta'(q_0, 0) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \text{ECLOSE}(q_0)} \delta(p, 0)\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\delta(q_0, 0) \cup \delta(q_1, 0)\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\{q_0\} \cup \varnothing\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_0\})$$ $$= \{q_0, q_1\}$$ **For state $q_0$, symbol $1$:** $$\delta'(q_0, 1) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\delta(q_0, 1) \cup \delta(q_1, 1)\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\varnothing \cup \{q_1\}\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_1\})$$ $$= \{q_1\}$$ **For state $q_1$, symbol $0$:** $$\delta'(q_1, 0) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\delta(q_0, 0) \cup \delta(q_1, 0)\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\{q_0\} \cup \varnothing\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_0\})$$ $$= \{q_0, q_1\}$$ **For state $q_1$, symbol $1$:** $$\delta'(q_1, 1) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\delta(q_0, 1) \cup \delta(q_1, 1)\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\varnothing \cup \{q_1\}\right)$$ $$= \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_1\})$$ $$= \{q_1\}$$ **Step 3 — Determine $F'$.** - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) = \{q_0, q_1\}$. This contains $q_1 \in F$, so $q_0 \in F'$. - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_1) = \{q_1\}$. This contains $q_1 \in F$, so $q_1 \in F'$. Therefore $F' = \{q_0, q_1\}$ (both states remain final). **Final Equivalent NFA $N$:** $$\delta'(q_0, 0) = \{q_0, q_1\}, \quad \delta'(q_0, 1) = \{q_1\}$$ $$\delta'(q_1, 0) = \{q_0, q_1\}, \quad \delta'(q_1, 1) = \{q_1\}$$ with $q_0$ as start and $F' = \{q_0, q_1\}$. > [!NOTE] > **Verification:** On input "0011" the original ε-NFA can be in $\{q_0, q_1\}$ (since $q_0$ is always final and $q_1$ is final too) — accepted. On input "10" the original ε-NFA cannot reach a final state because the $\varepsilon$-transition only allows $0 \to 1$ ordering — also matches the new NFA's behaviour. ✓ ### 3.3 Conversion Verification Matrix | Original ε-NFA Element | New NFA Equivalent | Reasoning | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | $\delta(q, \varepsilon) = \{p\}$ | Folded into $\delta'$ via $\text{ECLOSE}$ | Free jumps merged with each real step | | $q \in F$ (original final) | $q \in F'$ **iff** $\text{ECLOSE}(q) \cap F \neq \varnothing$ | A state becomes final if a final is reachable free of charge | | $\delta(q, a) = S$ | $\delta'(q, a) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \text{ECLOSE}(q)} \delta(p, a)\right)$ | Read $a$ from any free-jump neighbour, then jump free again | | $\varepsilon \in \Sigma$ of $E$ | $\varepsilon \notin \Sigma$ of $N$ | $\varepsilon$ is fully eliminated | ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 State Diagram — Original ε-NFA for $L = 0^* 1^*$ ```mermaid flowchart LR nodeQ0["q0 FINAL"] nodeQ1["q1 FINAL"] nodeQ0 -- "0" --> nodeQ0 nodeQ0 -. "epsilon" .-> nodeQ1 nodeQ1 -- "1" --> nodeQ1 ``` > [!NOTE] > **How to read this diagram:** A solid arrow `-->` denotes a transition consuming an input symbol; a dotted arrow `-.->` denotes an $\varepsilon$-transition (free teleport). Double-ringed or explicitly labelled "FINAL" nodes are accepting states. The self-loop on $q_0$ labelled `0` means any number of $0$s can be read in state $q_0$. The $\varepsilon$-arrow allows the machine to silently slip into $q_1$, after which only $1$s may be read. ### 4.2 State Diagram — Converted NFA (No Epsilon) ```mermaid flowchart LR stateQ0["q0 FINAL"] stateQ1["q1 FINAL"] stateQ0 -- "0" --> stateQ0 stateQ0 -- "0" --> stateQ1 stateQ1 -- "1" --> stateQ1 stateQ1 -- "0" --> stateQ0 ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **Observation from the diagram:** Compare the two diagrams carefully. The $\varepsilon$-arrow in the original has been *baked into* the symbol transitions of the new NFA. For example, the original had a free jump $q_0 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_1$ plus a self-loop $q_0 \xrightarrow{0} q_0$. The new NFA on reading `0` from $q_0$ can go to **both** $q_0$ and $q_1$ — effectively replicating the same behaviour without any free teleport. ### 4.3 Functional Architecture — ε-Elimination Pipeline ```mermaid flowchart LR inputA["Input epsilon NFA
Q Sigma delta q0 F"] stepA["Step 1
Compute ECLOSE of every state"] stepB["Step 2
Build new delta-prime using closure-union rule"] stepC["Step 3
Mark finals whose ECLOSE meets original F"] outputA["Output NFA
Q Sigma delta-prime q0 F-prime"] inputA --> stepA stepA --> stepB stepB --> stepC stepC --> outputA ``` > [!NOTE] > **Block-level interpretation:** The pipeline reads the original ε-NFA description, performs three deterministic transformations, and emits a clean NFA whose language is identical to the original. Every step is purely mechanical and can be hand-executed in an exam or automated in software. ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) --- **Q1. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`** Define an ε-NFA. How does it differ from a standard NFA? **Model Answer (3 marks):** An ε-NFA is a 5-tuple $E = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ where the transition function is $$\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \rightarrow 2^Q$$ The crucial difference from a standard NFA is that $\delta$ is defined on the **augmented input set** $\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}$, allowing the automaton to change state on the **empty string** without consuming any input symbol. A standard NFA can only transition on actual symbols from $\Sigma$. Both are non-deterministic; the new feature is the silent $\varepsilon$-move. *(Mark split: 1 mark for formal 5-tuple, 1 mark for mentioning $\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}$ in the domain, 1 mark for stating the silent-jump consequence.)* --- **Q2. `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`** What is the $\varepsilon$-closure of a state? Compute $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0)$ for the ε-NFA where $\delta(q_0, \varepsilon) = \{q_1, q_2\}$, $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \{q_3\}$, and no other $\varepsilon$-transitions exist. **Model Answer (3 marks):** The **$\varepsilon$-closure** of a state $q$ is the set of all states reachable from $q$ using zero or more $\varepsilon$-transitions. It always includes $q$ itself. **Computation:** - Begin with $\{q_0\}$. - Add $\delta(q_0, \varepsilon) = \{q_1, q_2\}$, so the set becomes $\{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$. - Add $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \{q_3\}$, so the set becomes $\{q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3\}$. - Check $q_2$ and $q_3$: neither has an $\varepsilon$-transition. Stop. $$\boxed{\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) = \{q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3\}}$$ *(Mark split: 1 mark for definition, 2 marks for correct closure computation.)* --- ### 5.2 Part B — Full 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice) --- ### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Adapted]` **(a)** Construct an ε-NFA for the regular expression $R = (0 + 1)^* 0 1$ using Thompson's construction idea, and clearly mark all states and transitions. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Convert the following ε-NFA into an equivalent NFA without $\varepsilon$-transitions. | State | $0$ | $1$ | $\varepsilon$ | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | $\rightarrow q_0$ | $\{q_0, q_1\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\varnothing$ | | $q_1$ | $\varnothing$ | $\{q_2\}$ | $\{q_3\}$ | | $*q_2$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ | | $q_3$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ | $\{q_2\}$ | (*$\rightarrow$ marks start, $*$ marks final*) **(7 marks)** --- #### **Solution A(a) — Model Answer** Thompson's construction builds one sub-NFA per regex sub-expression and joins them with $\varepsilon$-transitions. ```mermaid flowchart LR stA(("new q0")) stB["q1"] stC(("q2")) stD["q3"] stE(("q4 FINAL")) stF(("new q5")) stG["q6"] stH(("q7")) stI(("q8 FINAL")) stA -- "epsilon" --> stB stB -- "epsilon" --> stC stC -- "epsilon" --> stF stA -- "epsilon" --> stF stF -- "epsilon" --> stG stF -- "epsilon" --> stH stG -- "0" --> stC stH -- "1" --> stE stC -- "0" --> stC stC -- "1" --> stC ``` **Description of the constructed ε-NFA:** - **Start state $q_0$.** Two $\varepsilon$-transitions leave $q_0$: one to the "loop" sub-NFA (which reads any number of $0$s and $1$s) and one that bypasses the loop (for the empty iteration of $*$). - **Loop sub-NFA** at $q_1$–$q_2$: self-loop on both $0$ and $1$, then $\varepsilon$-jump back to the bypass point and continue into the suffix. - **Suffix** $q_3 \xrightarrow{0} q_4 \xrightarrow{1} q_5$ (final), where $q_5$ is the unique accepting state. The language accepted is exactly $(0 + 1)^* 0 1$. *(Mark split: 3 marks for identifying sub-NFAs for $0+1$, $^*$, $0$, $1$; 2 marks for correct $\varepsilon$-wiring; 2 marks for labelling start, final, and verifying the language.)* --- #### **Solution A(b) — Model Answer** **Step 1: Compute $\varepsilon$-closures.** - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) = \{q_0\}$ (no $\varepsilon$-transitions out). - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_1) = \{q_1, q_2, q_3\}$: $q_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_3$, and $q_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_2$. Then $q_2$ has no $\varepsilon$-transitions. Stop. - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_2) = \{q_2\}$. - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_3) = \{q_3, q_2\}$: $q_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_2$. Then $q_2$ stops. **Step 2: Compute $\delta'$ using** $\delta'(q, a) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \text{ECLOSE}(q)} \delta(p, a)\right).$ **For $q_0$:** - $\delta'(q_0, 0) = \text{ECLOSE}(\delta(q_0, 0)) = \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_0, q_1\}) = \{q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3\}$. - $\delta'(q_0, 1) = \text{ECLOSE}(\delta(q_0, 1)) = \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_0\}) = \{q_0\}$. **For $q_1$:** - $\delta'(q_1, 0) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\delta(q_1, 0) \cup \delta(q_2, 0) \cup \delta(q_3, 0)\right) = \text{ECLOSE}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$. - $\delta'(q_1, 1) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\delta(q_1, 1) \cup \delta(q_2, 1) \cup \delta(q_3, 1)\right) = \text{ECLOSE}(\{q_2\}) = \{q_2\}$. **For $q_2$:** - $\delta'(q_2, 0) = \text{ECLOSE}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$. - $\delta'(q_2, 1) = \text{ECLOSE}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$. **For $q_3$:** - $\delta'(q_3, 0) = \text{ECLOSE}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$. - $\delta'(q_3, 1) = \text{ECLOSE}(\varnothing) = \varnothing$. **Step 3: Determine $F'$.** - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) = \{q_0\}$ — does not contain $q_2 \Rightarrow q_0 \notin F'$. - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_1) = \{q_1, q_2, q_3\}$ — contains $q_2 \Rightarrow q_1 \in F'$. - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_2) = \{q_2\}$ — contains $q_2 \Rightarrow q_2 \in F'$. - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_3) = \{q_3, q_2\}$ — contains $q_2 \Rightarrow q_3 \in F'$. Therefore $F' = \{q_1, q_2, q_3\}$. **Final Equivalent NFA:** | State | $0$ | $1$ | | :---: | :---: | :---: | | $\rightarrow q_0$ | $\{q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ | | $*q_1$ | $\varnothing$ | $\{q_2\}$ | | $*q_2$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ | | $*q_3$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ | *(Mark split: 2 marks for $\varepsilon$-closures, 3 marks for new $\delta'$ computation, 2 marks for correct $F'$.)* > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall:** > 1. **Forgetting to iterate closure computation** — Students often stop after one $\varepsilon$-hop and miss transitive jumps (e.g., $q_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_2$). Always draw the $\varepsilon$-graph and run a closure until a fixed point. > 2. **Mishandling $F'$** — A common error is to keep the original $F$ as the new final set. The correct rule is: a state $q$ is final in $N$ **iff** $\text{ECLOSE}(q)$ intersects the original $F$. Forgetting this loses the empty-string acceptance that an $\varepsilon$-jump from start might have provided. > 3. **Forgetting the union inside closure** — For $\delta'(q, a)$ you must union $\delta(p, a)$ over **all** $p$ in $\text{ECLOSE}(q)$, not just over $q$ alone. --- ### **Question B (14 Marks — Alternative Choice)** `[KTU University Exam - May 2023, Adapted]` **(a)** For the ε-NFA given below, compute the $\varepsilon$-closure of every state and list the language accepted by the automaton. **(7 marks)** ```mermaid flowchart LR nA["q0 FINAL"] nB["q1"] nA -- "a, b" --> nA nA -. "epsilon" .-> nB nB -- "a" --> nA ``` **Transition table for clarity:** | State | $a$ | $b$ | $\varepsilon$ | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | $\rightarrow *q_0$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\{q_1\}$ | | $q_1$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\varnothing$ | $\varnothing$ | **(b)** State and prove (by construction) the theorem: *Every ε-NFA has an equivalent NFA (without $\varepsilon$-transitions).* **(7 marks)** --- #### **Solution B(a) — Model Answer** **Step 1: Compute $\varepsilon$-closures.** - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0)$: Start with $\{q_0\}$. Add $\delta(q_0, \varepsilon) = \{q_1\}$. From $q_1$, $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \varnothing$, stop. $$\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) = \{q_0, q_1\}$$ - $\text{ECLOSE}(q_1)$: Start with $\{q_1\}$. $\delta(q_1, \varepsilon) = \varnothing$, stop. $$\text{ECLOSE}(q_1) = \{q_1\}$$ **Step 2: Identify the language via reasoning.** From $q_0$, the machine may either: - Stay at $q_0$ and read any combination of $a$'s and $b$'s (self-loop on both), or - Silently jump to $q_1$ (free of charge) and from there read exactly one $a$ to return to $q_0$. Because $q_0$ is final, the machine accepts the empty string $\varepsilon$ (via the trivial zero-symbol read with $q_0$ final). It also accepts any string of $a$s and $b$s, and any string that ends at $q_0$ after a free jump and an $a$ — but since $q_0$ can already be reached by reading symbols directly, every string in $\Sigma^* = \{a, b\}^*$ is accepted. $$L(E) = \{a, b\}^*$$ *(Mark split: 2 marks for closures, 3 marks for trace-based language identification, 2 marks for the final answer in set-builder form.)* --- #### **Solution B(b) — Model Answer** **Theorem.** For every ε-NFA $E = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$, there exists an NFA $N = (Q, \Sigma, \delta', q_0, F')$ with no $\varepsilon$-transitions such that $L(E) = L(N)$. **Proof (by construction).** Define $N$ as follows. 1. **Compute $\text{ECLOSE}(q)$ for every $q \in Q$** as in Section 2.3 (smallest fixed-point set under $\varepsilon$-jumps). 2. **Define $\delta'$ for all $q \in Q$ and $a \in \Sigma$:** $$\delta'(q, a) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \text{ECLOSE}(q)} \delta(p, a)\right)$$ 3. **Define** $F' = \{\, q \in Q \mid \text{ECLOSE}(q) \cap F \neq \varnothing \,\}$. The start state and state set are unchanged. **Claim.** For every $w \in \Sigma^*$, $$\hat{\delta}_N(q_0, w) = \hat{\delta}_E(q_0, w)$$ where the left side uses the standard NFA extended transition (no closure) and the right side uses the ε-NFA extended transition (with closure). The proof proceeds by induction on $|w|$. - **Base case ($w = \varepsilon$):** In $N$, $\hat{\delta}_N(q_0, \varepsilon) = \{q_0\}$. We need this to equal $\hat{\delta}_E(q_0, \varepsilon) = \text{ECLOSE}(q_0)$. Since $\text{ECLOSE}(q_0) \cap F \neq \varnothing$ would put $q_0 \in F'$ (correctly reflecting free acceptance of $\varepsilon$), and the rest of the construction ensures the two sets agree on non-final membership, the claim holds. - **Inductive step ($w = xa$):** Assume $\hat{\delta}_N(q_0, x) = \hat{\delta}_E(q_0, x) = S$. Then: $$\hat{\delta}_N(q_0, xa) = \bigcup_{q \in S} \delta'(q, a) = \bigcup_{q \in S} \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \text{ECLOSE}(q)} \delta(p, a)\right) = \hat{\delta}_E(q_0, xa)$$ The final equality uses the definition of $\hat{\delta}_E$ and the fact that $\text{ECLOSE}(\text{ECLOSE}(X)) = \text{ECLOSE}(X)$. ∎ **Conclusion.** $w \in L(N) \iff \hat{\delta}_N(q_0, w) \cap F' \neq \varnothing \iff \hat{\delta}_E(q_0, w) \cap F \neq \varnothing \iff w \in L(E).$ *(Mark split: 2 marks for theorem statement, 3 marks for construction, 2 marks for the induction-based correctness proof.)* > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall (for Question B):** > 1. **Confusing "NFA" with "DFA"** — The conversion yields an NFA (still possibly non-deterministic), **not** a DFA. Students who claim "we get an equivalent DFA" lose marks. > 2. **Skipping the induction** — The theorem requires a rigorous proof, not just an example. A worked example demonstrates but does not *prove* the general statement. > 3. **Missing the role of $F'$** — Acceptance on $\varepsilon$ in the original ε-NFA must be carried over correctly. If $q_0 \in F'$ is not justified, the empty-string acceptance is lost. --- ### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!IMPORTANT] > **High-Density Revision Checklist** - [ ] **ε-NFA formal definition:** 5-tuple $(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ with $\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \rightarrow 2^Q$. - [ ] **Epsilon ($\varepsilon$) is NEVER in $\Sigma$** — it is only added to the *domain* of $\delta$. - [ ] **ε-closure ECLOSE($q$):** all states reachable from $q$ using **zero or more** $\varepsilon$-transitions; always includes $q$ itself. - [ ] **ECLOSE is a fixed-point operation:** compute by repeatedly adding $\delta(p, \varepsilon)$ for newly added $p$ until no new state is added. - [ ] **Extended transition $\hat{\delta}$:** base case $\hat{\delta}(q, \varepsilon) = \text{ECLOSE}(q)$; step case applies the union-then-closure rule. - [ ] **Conversion formula (memorise this):** $$\delta'(q, a) = \text{ECLOSE}\!\left(\bigcup_{p \in \text{ECLOSE}(q)} \delta(p, a)\right)$$ - [ ] **New final set rule:** $F' = \{\, q \in Q \mid \text{ECLOSE}(q) \cap F \neq \varnothing \,\}$. - [ ] **Equivalence result:** Every ε-NFA $\equiv$ some NFA (Thompson's construction and the ε-elimination algorithm are constructive proofs). - [ ] **State set $Q$ and start state $q_0$ are unchanged** during ε-elimination; only $\delta$ and $F$ are modified. - [ ] **Engineering relevance:** Lexical analysers, regex engines, pattern matchers — all internally use ε-NFA-style automata built from regular expressions. - [ ] **Common exam trap:** Forgetting that an ε-NFA may accept the **empty string** when $q_0$ is final *or* reachable from $q_0$ via $\varepsilon$ to a final state. - [ ] **Distinguish carefully:** NFA (non-determinism on symbols) vs ε-NFA (non-determinism + free moves) — the latter is a strict superset capability. - [ ] **Diagrammatic convention:** Solid arrow for symbol transitions; **dotted** arrow for $\varepsilon$-transitions. - [ ] **Tip for time management in KTU exam:** Always compute the full ε-closure table first; every later step depends on it. A single missed closure invalidates all subsequent $\delta'$ values.

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Regular Expression (RE):** A Regular Expression over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is a formal expression recursively defined using the following rules:
> 1. **Base Cases:** $\emptyset$ (empty set), $\varepsilon$ (empty string), and any single symbol $a \in \Sigma$ are regular expressions.
> 2. **Inductive Cases:** If $R_1$ and $R_2$ are regular expressions, then so are:
>    - $R_1 + R_2$ (Union / Alternation)
>    - $R_1 \cdot R_2$ (Concatenation)
>    - $R_1^{*}$ (Kleene Star / Closure)
> 3. **Closure:** No other expressions are regular.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Kleene's Theorem (1956):** A language $L$ is regular **if and only if** there exists a Finite Automaton (FA) that accepts $L$. This establishes the equivalence of three representations:
>
> $$\text{Regular Expression} \iff \text{NFA (with } \varepsilon\text{-moves)} \iff \text{DFA}$$

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — "The Recipe to Machine Pipeline"

Imagine a **recipe** (Regular Expression) that tells you how to combine ingredients like "$a$", "$b$", and operations like "OR", "AND", "repeat as many times". The recipe is human-readable, but a **blender machine** (Finite Automaton) needs a precise set of switches, gears, and belts to physically execute the recipe. 

The conversion from RE to FA is essentially the act of **translating a recipe into a working machine's blueprint**. Each symbol becomes a "check", each $\cdot$ becomes a "pipe connection", each $+$ becomes a "branch valve", and $^{*}$ becomes a "loopback conveyor belt".

- **$\emptyset$** → A machine with **no paths** (accepts nothing)
- **$\varepsilon$** → A machine with a **single start-accept state** (accepts empty string)
- **$a$** → A machine with **two states** (start → accept on $a$)
- **$+$** → A machine with a **choice point** (non-deterministic split)
- **$\cdot$** → A machine with **sequential pipes** (concatenated transitions)
- **$^{*}$** → A machine with a **loopback wire** (ε-back to start)

### 1.3 Why This Conversion Matters in KTU 2024 Scheme

> [!NOTE]
> KTU examiners frequently test this topic because:
> - It directly maps to **Module 2 CO2**: "Construct FA equivalent to a given Regular Expression"
> - It tests **Apply** and **Analyze** levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
> - It builds foundation for **Pumping Lemma** (Module 3) and **Context-Free Grammars** (Module 4)

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The McNaughton-Yamada Construction Algorithm

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **McNaughton-Yamada Algorithm (1960):** Also known as **Thompson's Construction**. This is the standard KTU-approved method to convert any Regular Expression $R$ into an equivalent $\varepsilon$-NFA, denoted as $N(R)$, satisfying:
> $$\mathcal{L}(N(R)) = \mathcal{L}(R)$$

The construction proceeds **recursively** following the structure of $R$, applying base-case NFAs to leaf operands and combining sub-NFAs for operators.

### 2.2 Base Case NFAs (Atomic Blocks)

| Case | Regular Expression | States in $N(R)$ | Start State | Accept State | Transitions | Accepts |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | $\emptyset$ | 1 | $q_0$ | (none) | None | $\emptyset$ |
| 2 | $\varepsilon$ | 1 | $q_0$ | $q_0$ | None | $\{\varepsilon\}$ |
| 3 | $a \in \Sigma$ | 2 | $q_0$ | $q_1$ | $\delta(q_0, a) = q_1$ | $\{a\}$ |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Golden Rule:** Every accept state in the constructed NFA must have **exactly one incoming path** and **no outgoing transitions**. This is what makes Thompson's NFAs have **at most $2|R|$ states**, where $\vert R \vert$ is the length of the regular expression.

### 2.3 Inductive Case NFAs (Combinators)

Let $N(R_1)$ and $N(R_2)$ be the NFAs for $R_1$ and $R_2$ with start states $s_1, s_2$ and accept states $f_1, f_2$ respectively.

#### A. Union: $R = R_1 + R_2$
1. Create a **new start state** $s$ and a **new accept state** $f$.
2. Add $\varepsilon$-transitions: $s \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_1$, $s \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_2$, $f_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f$, $f_2 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f$.

#### B. Concatenation: $R = R_1 \cdot R_2$
1. Merge $f_1$ (accept of $R_1$) with $s_2$ (start of $R_2$).
2. Effectively: connect $f_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_2$.
3. The new start is $s_1$; the new accept is $f_2$.

#### C. Kleene Star: $R = R_1^{*}$
1. Create new start state $s$ and new accept state $f$.
2. Add $\varepsilon$-transitions:
   - $s \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f$ (accept empty string)
   - $s \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_1$ (enter the loop)
   - $f_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_1$ (loop back)
   - $f_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f$ (exit after one or more iterations)

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Property | Mathematical Statement | Engineering Utility |
|:--|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | RE $\Leftrightarrow$ NFA | $\mathcal{L}(N(R)) = \mathcal{L}(R)$ | Compiler regex engines (lex, flex) |
| 2 | State Bound | States in $N(R) \leq 2 \cdot \text{length}(R)$ | Lexical analyzer size estimation |
| 3 | NFA $\to$ DFA (Subset) | $Q_{DFA} \subseteq 2^{Q_{NFA}}$ | Deterministic simulation of NFA |
| 4 | State Explosion | $\vert Q_{DFA} \vert \leq 2^{\vert Q_{NFA} \vert}$ | Worst-case: $2^n$ states |
| 5 | Epsilon Closure | $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(q) = \{p \mid q \Rightarrow^{*} p\}$ | Used in NFA simulation |
| 6 | Union Size | $\mathcal{L}(R_1 + R_2) = \mathcal{L}(R_1) \cup \mathcal{L}(R_2)$ | Choice in pattern matching |
| 7 | Concatenation Size | $\mathcal{L}(R_1 \cdot R_2) = \{xy \mid x \in \mathcal{L}(R_1), y \in \mathcal{L}(R_2)\}$ | Sequence matching |
| 8 | Kleene Star | $\mathcal{L}(R^{*}) = \bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty} \mathcal{L}(R)^i$ | Repetition matching |

### 2.5 Engineering Real-World Utility

- **Lexical Analyzers (Lex/Flex):** Compilers convert regex tokens (e.g., `\d+`, `[a-zA-Z_]\w*`) to NFAs, then to DFAs for fast input scanning.
- **Network Intrusion Detection Systems (Snort):** Use regex-to-FA conversion to match packet patterns at line speed.
- **DNA Sequence Matching (Bioinformatics):** Convert biological pattern regexes into finite automata for genome scanning.
- **Search Engines (grep/egrep):** POSIX regex libraries internally use Thompson's NFA construction.
- **Model Checking:** Hardware verification tools convert LTL/regular property formulas to automata.

### 2.6 From NFA to DFA — The Subset Construction

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Subset Construction (Rabin-Scott, 1959):** Since deterministic machines are easier to implement in hardware/software, the $\varepsilon$-NFA from Thompson's construction is converted to a DFA. Each DFA state represents a **set of NFA states** reachable via $\varepsilon$-transitions.

Given $N = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ with $\varepsilon$-moves, construct DFA $D = (Q', \Sigma, \delta', q'_0, F')$:
- $q'_0 = \varepsilon\text{-closure}(q_0)$
- $Q' = 2^Q$ (subsets of NFA states)
- $F' = \{S \in Q' \mid S \cap F \neq \emptyset\}$
- $\delta'(S, a) = \varepsilon\text{-closure}\!\left(\bigcup_{q \in S} \delta(q, a)\right)$

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Comprehensive Worked Example: $R = (a + b)^* a b$

This is a **classic KTU textbook problem**. The language accepted is: *all strings over $\{a, b\}$ that end in "$ab$"*. We will build the $\varepsilon$-NFA step-by-step.

#### Step 1 — Identify Sub-Expressions

$$R = (a + b)^* \cdot a \cdot b$$

Sub-expressions in order of dependency:
- $R_1 = a$ (base case)
- $R_2 = b$ (base case)
- $R_3 = a + b$ (union of $R_1$ and $R_2$)
- $R_4 = R_3^{*} = (a+b)^{*}$ (Kleene star of $R_3$)
- $R_5 = R_4 \cdot a$ (concatenation of $R_4$ and $R_1$)
- $R_6 = R_5 \cdot b$ (concatenation of $R_5$ and $R_2$)

#### Step 2 — Build NFA for $R_1 = a$

$$\begin{aligned}
N(R_1) &: \text{States} = \{p_0, p_1\} \\
\text{Start} &= p_0, \quad \text{Accept} = p_1 \\
\delta(p_0, a) &= p_1
\end{aligned}$$

#### Step 3 — Build NFA for $R_2 = b$

$$\begin{aligned}
N(R_2) &: \text{States} = \{q_0, q_1\} \\
\text{Start} &= q_0, \quad \text{Accept} = q_1 \\
\delta(q_0, b) &= q_1
\end{aligned}$$

#### Step 4 — Build NFA for $R_3 = R_1 + R_2$ (Union)

Create new start $s_3$ and new accept $f_3$:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{States added}&: \{s_3, f_3\} \\
\text{New } \delta&: s_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} p_0, \quad s_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_0, \quad p_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f_3, \quad q_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f_3 \\
\text{Start} &= s_3, \quad \text{Accept} = f_3
\end{aligned}$$

#### Step 5 — Build NFA for $R_4 = R_3^{*}$ (Kleene Star)

Create new start $s_4$ and new accept $f_4$:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{New } \delta&: s_4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f_4, \quad s_4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_3, \quad f_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s_3, \quad f_3 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f_4 \\
\text{Start} &= s_4, \quad \text{Accept} = f_4
\end{aligned}$$

#### Step 6 — Build NFA for $R_5 = R_4 \cdot R_1$ (Concatenation)

Connect accept of $R_4$ to start of $R_1$:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{New } \delta&: f_4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} p_0 \quad \text{(merge } f_4 \text{ with } p_0) \\
\text{Start} &= s_4, \quad \text{Accept} = p_1
\end{aligned}$$

#### Step 7 — Build NFA for $R_6 = R_5 \cdot R_2$ (Concatenation)

Connect accept of $R_5$ to start of $R_2$:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{New } \delta&: p_1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_0 \quad \text{(merge } p_1 \text{ with } q_0) \\
\text{Start} &= s_4, \quad \text{Accept} = q_1
\end{aligned}$$

#### Step 8 — State Renumbering (Standard KTU Convention)

After relabeling, the complete $\varepsilon$-NFA has **6 states**:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{States} &= \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} \\
\text{Start} &= 1, \quad \text{Accept} = \{6\} \\
\Sigma &= \{a, b\} \\
\delta(1, \varepsilon) &= \{2, 5\} \quad \text{(skip-to-accept or enter loop)} \\
\delta(2, \varepsilon) &= \{3, 6\} \quad \text{(enter a-branch or skip)} \\
\delta(3, a) &= \{4\} \\
\delta(4, \varepsilon) &= \{2, 5\} \quad \text{(loopback or exit to } a\text{-branch)} \\
\delta(5, b) &= \{6\}
\end{aligned}$$

**State Count Verification:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Number of symbols} &= 4 \;(a, b, a, b) \\
\text{Operators} &= 3 \;(+, ^{*}, \cdot, \cdot) \\
\text{Total } \vert R \vert &= 4 + 3 = 7 \\
\text{States} &\leq 2 \cdot 7 = 14 \;\; \checkmark \text{ (we have 6, well within bound)}
\end{aligned}$$

### 3.2 Analytical Matrix — Subset Construction (NFA → DFA)

Apply subset construction to the above NFA. Compute $\varepsilon$-closures first:

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon\text{-closure}(1) &= \{1, 2, 3, 6, 5\} \\
\varepsilon\text{-closure}(2) &= \{2, 3, 6\} \\
\varepsilon\text{-closure}(3) &= \{3\} \\
\varepsilon\text{-closure}(4) &= \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} \\
\varepsilon\text{-closure}(5) &= \{5, 6\} \\
\varepsilon\text{-closure}(6) &= \{6\}
\end{aligned}$$

Now construct the DFA transition table:

| DFA State | NFA Subset | $\delta(\cdot, a)$ | $\delta(\cdot, b)$ | Accept? |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $A$ | $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 6\}$ | $C$ | $B$ | **Yes** (contains 6) |
| $B$ | $\{4, 5, 6\}$ | $C$ | $B$ | **Yes** (contains 6) |
| $C$ | $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ | $C$ | $B$ | **Yes** (contains 6) |

Since $A$ and $B$ have identical transitions to $C$ and $B$, and $C$ loops to itself on $a$, the **minimized DFA** collapses to 3 states.

### 3.3 Verification: String Acceptance Test

Test string $w = \text{``}aab\text{''}$ (should be accepted since it ends in $ab$):

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Path trace:} \quad & q_0 = 1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3 \xrightarrow{a} 4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3 \xrightarrow{a} 4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 5 \xrightarrow{b} 6 \;\; \in F \\
&\therefore \text{``}aab\text{''} \in \mathcal{L}(N) \;\; \checkmark
\end{aligned}$$

Test string $w = \text{``}ba\text{''}$ (should be rejected since it ends in $a$):

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Path trace:} \quad & 1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 5 \xrightarrow{b} 6 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} \cdots \text{ no } a \text{ from } 6 \\
&\text{Or: } 1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 2 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 6 \;\; \text{Then stuck — no outgoing on } a \\
&\therefore \text{``}ba\text{''} \notin \mathcal{L}(N) \;\; \checkmark
\end{aligned}$$

### 3.4 Worked Example 2: $R = (ab + a)^{*}$ — Unary/Trace Walk

Sub-expressions: $a, b, ab, ab + a, (ab + a)^{*}$.

- **$R_1 = a$:** 2 states ($1 \xrightarrow{a} 2$)
- **$R_2 = b$:** 2 states ($3 \xrightarrow{b} 4$)
- **$R_3 = ab$:** Concatenate $R_1, R_2$ → states $1 \xrightarrow{a} 2 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3 \xrightarrow{b} 4$ (start 1, accept 4)
- **$R_4 = ab + a$:** Union — new start $s$, new accept $f$; $\varepsilon$-transitions from $s$ to $1$ and $1$ (for $R_1$), and from accept states (4 and 2) to $f$.
- **$R_5 = R_4^{*}$:** Apply Kleene star — new start $s'$, new accept $f'$; add $s' \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f'$ (empty string accepted), $s' \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s$, $f \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} s$, $f \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} f'$.

The accept language: zero or more occurrences of "$ab$" or "$a$" — i.e., any string where $a$ always appears in blocks of "$ab$" or single "$a$", but never bare "$b$" or "$ba$".

#### Question 1: Define Regular Expression. Construct NFA for the RE $R = a \cdot b^{*}$. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Model Answer:**

> [!NOTE]
> A Regular Expression over alphabet $\Sigma$ is a formal expression built from $\emptyset$, $\varepsilon$, symbols in $\Sigma$, and operators $+$ (union), $\cdot$ (concatenation), and $^{*}$ (Kleene star).

**Construction of NFA for $R = ab^{*}$:**

Step 1 — NFA for $a$: States $\{1, 2\}$, $\delta(1, a) = 2$, start = $1$, accept = $2$.

Step 2 — NFA for $b$: States $\{3, 4\}$, $\delta(3, b) = 4$, start = $3$, accept = $4$.

Step 3 — NFA for $b^{*}$: Apply Kleene star with new start $5$ and accept $6$:
- $5 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 6$ (accept $\varepsilon$)
- $5 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3$ (enter)
- $4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3$ (loop)
- $4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 6$ (exit)

Step 4 — Concatenation $a \cdot b^{*}$: Connect $2 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 5$. Final NFA has **6 states**, start = $1$, accept = $6$.

```mermaid
    n5 -- epsilon --> n6((6))
```

#### Question 2: State Kleene's Theorem and explain its significance. `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Model Answer:**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Kleene's Theorem (1956):** A language $L$ is **regular if and only if** it is accepted by some Finite Automaton.
>
> Formally:
> $$\text{Regular Language} \iff \text{Exists DFA } M \text{ such that } \mathcal{L}(M) = L$$

**Significance:**
1. Establishes **equivalence** between three representations: RE, NFA, and DFA.
2. Provides **constructive algorithms** to convert between them.
3. Forms the theoretical foundation for **regex engines** in compilers.
4. Enables **decidability** results in formal language theory.

---

### Part B Questions (14 Marks Each)

#### Question A (14 Marks): `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**(a)** Construct an $\varepsilon$-NFA for the Regular Expression $R = (a + b)^{*} b a$ using McNaughton-Yamada construction. Show all intermediate steps. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

Sub-expressions:
- $R_1 = a$, $R_2 = b$ (base cases)
- $R_3 = a + b$ (union)
- $R_4 = (a + b)^{*}$ (Kleene star)
- $R_5 = R_4 \cdot b$ (concatenation)
- $R_6 = R_5 \cdot a$ (concatenation)

**NFA for $R_1 = a$:** States $1, 2$; $\delta(1, a) = 2$.

**NFA for $R_2 = b$:** States $3, 4$; $\delta(3, b) = 4$.

**NFA for $R_3 = a + b$:** New start $5$, new accept $6$:
- $5 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 1$ (enter $a$-branch)
- $5 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3$ (enter $b$-branch)
- $2 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 6$, $4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 6$ (merge accepts)

**NFA for $R_4 = R_3^{*}$:** New start $7$, new accept $8$:
- $7 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 8$ (accept $\varepsilon$)
- $7 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 5$ (enter)
- $6 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 5$ (loop)
- $6 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 8$ (exit)

**NFA for $R_5 = R_4 \cdot b$:** Connect $8 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 3$. New start = $7$, accept = $4$.

**NFA for $R_6 = R_5 \cdot a$:** Connect $4 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 1$. New start = $7$, accept = $2$.

**Final $\varepsilon$-NFA:**

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\} \\
q_0 &= 7, \quad F = \{2\} \\
\delta(7, \varepsilon) &= \{5, 8\} \\
\delta(5, \varepsilon) &= \{1, 3\} \\
\delta(1, a) &= \{2\} \\
\delta(3, b) &= \{4\} \\
\delta(2, \varepsilon) &= \{6\} \\
\delta(4, \varepsilon) &= \{1, 6\} \\
\delta(6, \varepsilon) &= \{5, 8\}
\end{aligned}$$

**State count check:** $\vert R \vert = 7$, so $\vert Q \vert \leq 14$. We have $8 \leq 14$ ✓.

```mermaid

    q7 -- epsilon --> q8((8))

    q5 -- epsilon --> q3((3))

    q3 -- b --> q4((4))
    q2 -- epsilon --> q6((6))
```

**(b)** Convert the above $\varepsilon$-NFA to an equivalent DFA using subset construction. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

Compute $\varepsilon$-closures:
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(7) = \{5, 7, 8, 1, 3\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(5) = \{1, 3, 5\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(8) = \{8\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(1) = \{1\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(3) = \{3\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(6) = \{5, 6, 8, 1, 3\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(2) = \{2, 6, 5, 8, 1, 3\}$
- $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(4) = \{1, 3, 4, 6, 5, 8\}$

| DFA State | NFA Subset | On $a$ | On $b$ | Accept? |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $A$ (start) | $\{1, 3, 5, 7, 8\}$ | $C$ | $D$ | No |
| $C$ | $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$ | $C$ | $D$ | **Yes** (contains 2) |
| $D$ | $\{1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$ | $C$ | $D$ | **Yes** (contains 6, 8) |
| $B$ | $\{1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$ — same as $D$ | merged | merged | — |

$$\begin{aligned}
\delta(A, a) &= C, \quad \delta(A, b) = D \\
\delta(C, a) &= C, \quad \delta(C, b) = D \\
\delta(D, a) &= C, \quad \delta(D, b) = D
\end{aligned}$$

The language: all strings ending in "$ba$" — since only after reading "$ba$" do we reach state $C$ (accept).

#### Question B (14 Marks): `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**(a)** For the Regular Expression $R = (0 + 1)^{*} 0 0 (0 + 1)^{*}$, explain in detail the language it represents and construct its equivalent $\varepsilon$-NFA using Thompson's construction. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Language Description:** The set of all binary strings that contain the substring "$00$" at least once.

Formally:

$$\mathcal{L}(R) = \{w \in \{0,1\}^{*} \mid w \text{ contains } 00 \text{ as a substring}\}$$

Examples in language: $00$, $100$, $001$, $000$, $1001$, $1100110$.  
Examples NOT in language: $\varepsilon$, $0$, $1$, $01$, $10$, $0101$, $10101$.

**Thompson's Construction:**

Sub-expressions:
- $R_1 = 0$, $R_2 = 1$ (base cases, 2 states each)
- $R_3 = 0 + 1$ (union — 4 + 2 = 6 states)
- $R_4 = (0 + 1)^{*}$ (Kleene star — adds 2 states → 8 states)
- $R_5 = R_4 \cdot 0$ (concatenation)
- $R_6 = R_5 \cdot 0$ (concatenation)
- $R_7 = R_6 \cdot (0 + 1)^{*}$ (concatenation with $R_4$)

**State-by-state NFA:**

After relabeling, the final $\varepsilon$-NFA has **8 states** with the following key transitions:

$$\begin{aligned}
\delta(1, \varepsilon) &= \{2, 5\} \quad \text{(skip to accept or start loop)} \\
\delta(2, \varepsilon) &= \{3, 7\} \quad \text{(enter 0-branch or 1-branch of union)} \\
\delta(3, 0) &= \{4\}, \quad \delta(7, 1) &= \{8\} \\
\delta(4, \varepsilon) &= \{5, 6\} \quad \text{(merge accepts of union)} \\
\delta(6, \varepsilon) &= \{2, 5\} \quad \text{(loopback in star)} \\
\delta(5, 0) &= \{6\} \quad \text{(first "0" of "00")} \\
\delta(6, 0) &= \{2, 5, 9\} \quad \text{(second "0" — proceed to final } (0+1)^{*} \text{)} \\
\delta(9, \varepsilon) &= \{2, 5\} \quad \text{(loop in final star)}
\end{aligned}$$

Final start = $1$, final accept = $5$ (with $1 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} 5$ for the "skip to accept" branch of Kleene star).

```mermaid
    n2 -- epsilon --> n3((3))
    n2 -- epsilon --> n7((7))

    n7 -- 1 --> n8((8))
```

**(b)** Convert the above $\varepsilon$-NFA to its equivalent DFA using subset construction algorithm. List all states, transitions, and identify start and final states. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

After computing $\varepsilon$-closures for all 10 states, the subset construction yields:

| DFA State | NFA Subset | On $0$ | On $1$ | Accept? |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $A$ | $\{1, 2, 5\}$ | $B$ | $C$ | No |
| $B$ | $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ | $D$ | $C$ | No |
| $C$ | $\{1, 2, 5, 7, 8\}$ | $B$ | $C$ | No |
| $D$ | $\{1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10\}$ | $E$ | $C$ | **Yes** (contains 5) |
| $E$ | $\{1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10\}$ (same as $D$) | $E$ | $C$ | **Yes** (contains 5) |

So $D$ and $E$ are equivalent — they merge. **Final DFA: 4 states** $\{A, B, C, D\}$, start = $A$, accept = $\{D\}$.

### KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Deduction Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Forgetting $\varepsilon$-transitions in Kleene Star:** Many students forget the four $\varepsilon$-moves ($s \to f$, $s \to s_1$, $f_1 \to s_1$, $f_1 \to f$). This causes the FA to **NOT** accept $\varepsilon$ for the $R^{*}$ case — **lose 2 marks**.
> 2. **Wrong merge in Concatenation:** In $R_1 \cdot R_2$, the accept of $R_1$ must merge with start of $R_2$ via $\varepsilon$. Some students add an extra state — **lose 1 mark** for not following Thompson's standard.
> 3. **Not labeling $\varepsilon$ explicitly:** Every $\varepsilon$-transition must be clearly marked. Unlabeled transitions are interpreted as **no transition** by examiners — **lose 1–2 marks**.
> 4. **Subset Construction errors:** Confusing the "current subset" with "$\varepsilon$-closure of current subset" is a frequent error. Always apply $\varepsilon$-closure **after** every transition — **lose 2–3 marks**.
> 5. **Forget to mark accept states with double circles** in diagrams — **lose 1 mark** for not following KTU diagram conventions.
> 6. **In RE evaluation, write $a^{+}$ as a single operator:** KTU expects $a^{+} = a \cdot a^{*}$. Writing $a^{+}$ as primitive loses **1 mark** unless explicitly defined as such in your answer.
> 7. **State count not verified:** Always verify $\vert Q \vert \leq 2 \cdot \text{length}(R)$ to catch errors.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **RE $\Leftrightarrow$ NFA $\Leftrightarrow$ DFA:** All three represent the same class of **regular languages** (Kleene's Theorem).
- **McNaughton-Yamada (Thompson's) Construction** is the standard KTU method: build NFA **recursively from leaves to root** of the parse tree.
- **Base Cases (3):** $\emptyset \to 1$ state, $\varepsilon \to 1$ state (start = accept), $a \to 2$ states.
- **Inductive Cases (3):** Union ($+$): 2 new states + 4 $\varepsilon$-moves; Concatenation ($\cdot$): 1 $\varepsilon$-merge; Kleene Star ($^{*}$): 2 new states + 4 $\varepsilon$-moves.
- **State Count Bound:** $\vert Q_{NFA} \vert \leq 2 \cdot \text{length}(R)$.
- **Epsilon-Closure:** $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(q)$ is the set of all states reachable from $q$ using only $\varepsilon$-transitions (including $q$ itself).
- **Subset Construction (Rabin-Scott):** Each DFA state = a subset of NFA states. Start state = $\varepsilon\text{-closure}(q_0)$. Accept states = subsets containing any NFA accept state.
- **State Explosion:** In worst case, NFA with $n$ states can convert to DFA with $2^n$ states.
- **Accept State Convention:** In diagrams, accept states are drawn as **double circles**.
- **Kleene's Theorem is the bridge** between theoretical RE and practical FA implementations.
- **Practical Use:** Lex/Flex (compilers), grep/egrep, Snort (IDS), DNA matching, hardware model checking.
- **Precedence in RE (highest to lowest):** $^{*}$ (star), $\cdot$ (concatenation), $+$ (union). Use parentheses to override.
